name: Kewzing
tagline: A Bhutia village where homestay income is shared
meta_description: Kewzing, South Sikkim: community homestays near Ravangla, the Bon monastery, village walks, cardamom and farm life, how to reach and honest 2026 costs.
summary: Kewzing is a Bhutia farming village at about 1,550 m, roughly 9–10 km and 25 minutes below Ravangla on the road to Legship. It is known for a community homestay programme started in 2003, run by a village committee that shares guests between families, and for a Bon monastery, one of very few in India.
intro: Kewzing lies on the slope west of Ravangla, where the road drops through cardamom, maize and vegetable plots towards Legship and the Rangeet. Most households are Bhutia Buddhist families who still farm, and prayer flags and small chortens mark the paths between houses. At about 1,550 m it is a little warmer than Ravangla, and on clear mornings Kangchenjunga, Kabru and Narsing show above the West Sikkim hills.

What makes Kewzing different is how its tourism works. In 2003 villagers began hosting guests in their own homes, and they formed an elected body, the Kewzing Tourism Development Committee, to spread visitors fairly between participating families rather than letting one or two homes take every booking. Down To Earth magazine reported on the model as an example of community tourism in Sikkim. For you, that means a simple room, home-cooked food and a host who can explain the village.

Kewzing is also home to a Bon monastery. Bon is the religious tradition that predates Buddhism in Tibet and continues alongside it, and Bon monasteries are rare in India. Add a monastery walk, farm work in season and an easy drive to Ravangla's Buddha Park and Ralang, and Kewzing makes a good two-night stop between Pelling and Namchi.

story.title: Bon, the older faith of the Tibetan world
story.text: Visitors to Kewzing often assume every monastery in Sikkim is Buddhist. One here is not. Bon is the indigenous religious tradition of Tibet, older than the arrival of Buddhism in the 7th and 8th centuries, and it survived the centuries in which Buddhism became dominant. Wikipedia's article on Bon describes how the modern tradition, sometimes called Yungdrung Bon, developed its own canon, monasteries and monastic training, and traces its teachings to a founder figure named Tonpa Shenrab Miwoche rather than to the Buddha. To an outsider a Bon temple looks much like a Buddhist one: prayer flags, butter lamps, painted murals and monks in maroon robes. Look closer and the differences show. Bon practitioners walk around shrines and turn prayer wheels anticlockwise, the reverse of Buddhist practice, and the swastika, an ancient symbol of permanence, points the other way. Kewzing's small Bon monastery serves the local followers of this tradition. Visit quietly, follow the lead of the caretaker, and when you circle the shrine, ask which way to walk.
story.source: Wikipedia: Bon; Kewzing village, as told locally

little_known.fact: Kewzing's homestays are allocated by an elected village body, the Kewzing Tourism Development Committee, so income is shared between families rather than concentrated in a few homes.
In Bon practice, shrines and stupas are circled anticlockwise, the opposite of the clockwise walk used at Buddhist monasteries such as nearby Ralang.
The road through Kewzing links Ravangla with Legship on the Rangeet, the usual route for cars driving between Ravangla and Pelling, about 45–50 km in all.

facts: Community homestays, Bon monastery, farm life
Not needed for Indians; foreigners need the Sikkim RAP

highlights.title: Community homestays
highlights.text: Sleep in a Bhutia family home under a programme the village has run since 2003. A village committee shares guests between families. Rooms are simple and clean, meals are home-cooked, and hosts are farmers who can show you their fields and kitchens. About ₹1,500–2,500 per person a night with meals.

highlights.title: Kewzing's Bon monastery
highlights.text: A small monastery of the Bon tradition, which predates Buddhism in Tibet. Bon monasteries are rare in India. Visit quietly with your host, remove shoes inside and ask which way to circle the shrine: Bon practice goes anticlockwise.

highlights.title: Monastery and viewpoint walk
highlights.text: Your host can point you to a walking route that links Kewzing's monasteries, chortens and viewpoints in two to three gentle hours. Kangchenjunga and Narsing show above the West Sikkim hills on clear mornings from October to February.

highlights.title: Cardamom season
highlights.text: From about August to November, families pick large cardamom in the shaded gullies and dry the pods in smoky kilns. Ask to watch or help. Sikkim is India's largest producer of large cardamom, and it is the main cash crop for many Kewzing households.

highlights.title: Twenty minutes to Ravangla
highlights.text: Buddha Park and its 130 ft Buddha, the Ralang monasteries and the Maenam forest trail are all a short drive up the hill, so Kewzing works as a quieter base for Ravangla sightseeing, and as an overnight on the road between Pelling and Namchi.

how_to_reach.text: Shared jeeps between Ravangla and Legship pass through Kewzing during the day for about ₹50–100 a seat, and Ravangla is about 3 hours from Gangtok by shared jeep at ₹250–400. Ask the driver to drop you at Kewzing and call your host. Fares are indicative; check current status before you travel.

A reserved small car from Ravangla costs about ₹600–900 for the 9–10 km. From Gangtok a car straight to Kewzing costs about ₹4,000–5,000, and from Pelling, about 35–40 km via Legship, roughly ₹2,500–3,500. Many guests stop here on a Pelling–Ravangla–Namchi loop.

About 130 km and 5 hours via NH10, Melli, Namchi and Ravangla, or via Jorethang and Legship, for about ₹6,000–7,500 by reserved car. When NH10 is closed by monsoon slides, drivers route through Darjeeling district and Jorethang, which suits Kewzing well.

where_to_stay: Most visitors stay in the village homestays, booked through the community programme, at about ₹1,500–2,500 per person a night with meals; we match guests to families we know. For a little more comfort, Bon Farmhouse is a family-run farmstay among tea, cardamom and vegetable fields near the Bon monastery, at about ₹3,000–5,500 a room. Ravangla, 20–25 minutes up the hill, has hotels such as Mt. Narsing Village Resort and The Barfung Retreat.
tips: Book homestays a few weeks ahead from October to December and in April–May; each home has only one to three rooms.
Tell your host about dietary needs before you arrive, as meals are cooked for the household and guests together.
At the Bon monastery, ask which way to walk before circling the shrine; it differs from Buddhist practice.
Carry cash for homestays and small purchases; withdraw in Ravangla, Namchi or Gangtok.
Pack a light down jacket from November to February: nights drop to about 4–7 °C even though days are sunny.

experiences.title: Visit Kewzing's Bon monastery with your host
experiences.summary: A quiet visit to one of very few Bon monasteries in India, guided by your homestay host. Learn how the Bon tradition, older than Buddhism in Tibet, differs in practice from the Buddhist monasteries you see elsewhere in Sikkim, starting with which way you walk around the shrine.
body: Bon is the indigenous religious tradition of Tibet, older than the arrival of Buddhism, and it continues today with its own monasteries, scriptures and monks. Wikipedia's article on Bon traces its teachings to Tonpa Shenrab Miwoche. In Sikkim, where nearly every monastery is Buddhist, a Bon temple is unusual, and Kewzing's is the reason many curious travellers come here.

From outside it looks familiar: prayer flags, a small courtyard, painted doors and butter lamps. The differences are in the details. Bon followers circle shrines and turn prayer wheels anticlockwise, and the swastika symbol points the opposite way to the Buddhist one. The deities on the murals belong to the Bon pantheon.

Go with your host, who can find the caretaker and explain what you see. Remove shoes and hats inside, dress modestly and ask before taking photographs. A small donation at the altar is customary. Opening is informal, so morning is the most reliable time to find someone there.

faqs.q: What is a Bon monastery?
faqs.a: A Bon monastery follows Bon, the religious tradition that existed in Tibet before Buddhism arrived and has continued alongside it. It has its own monks, scriptures and rituals. Visually it resembles a Buddhist monastery, but practices such as circling shrines anticlockwise and the direction of the swastika symbol differ.

faqs.q: Can tourists visit the Bon monastery in Kewzing?
faqs.a: Yes, respectfully and ideally with your homestay host, who can find the caretaker. There is no ticket. Remove your shoes and hat inside, keep your voice low, ask before photographing, and leave a small donation if you wish. Opening hours are informal, so go in the morning.

faqs.q: Which way should we walk around a Bon shrine?
faqs.a: Anticlockwise, the reverse of the clockwise walk at Buddhist monasteries such as Ralang or Rumtek. If you are unsure, watch the local people or ask the caretaker. Nobody expects visitors to know every custom, but asking shows respect and usually starts a good conversation.

experiences.title: Kewzing's monastery and chorten trail
experiences.cost: Free, or ≈ ₹300–600 for a local guide
experiences.image_query: prayer flags village trail Ravangla Sikkim
experiences.summary: A gentle morning loop on village paths linking Kewzing's monasteries, chortens and viewpoints, with Kangchenjunga and Narsing above the West Sikkim hills on clear days. Easy enough for families, with tea at home afterwards.
body: Village walks are the heart of a Kewzing stay. A loop of paths links the village's monasteries, prayer-flag ridges and viewpoints across the Rangeet valley, and can be walked in two to three hours at a gentle pace. Your host will point out the start or send someone along with you.

Expect quiet lanes between houses, short climbs through cardamom and maize, chortens wrapped in prayer flags and the occasional mani wall, which you pass keeping it on your right. On clear mornings from October to February, Kangchenjunga, Kabru and Narsing rise to the north-west, and the birding along the field edges is good in spring.

Start early for the clearest views and coolest air. Wear shoes with grip, carry water and a rain jacket, and stay on established paths through fields. Trails shift after each monsoon, so ask your host about the route before setting out.

faqs.q: How long is the Kewzing village walk?
faqs.a: Most people take two to three hours at an easy pace, including stops at monasteries and viewpoints. The paths are mostly gentle with a few short climbs. You can shorten it easily by turning back at any point, since the village is compact and your homestay is never far away.

faqs.q: Do we need a guide for the Kewzing walk?
faqs.a: Not strictly, but a host or local guide makes it far more interesting and stops you taking a wrong turn through private fields. A guide costs about ₹300–600 per group, indicative. They can explain the monasteries, name the peaks and show you crops in season.

faqs.q: Is the walk suitable for older travellers?
faqs.a: Yes, for those comfortable walking on uneven paths for an hour or two. There are no long or steep climbs on the main loop, and you can rest at monasteries along the way. Walking poles help on the descents. Avoid it after heavy rain when paths turn slippery.

experiences.title: A cardamom and farm day with a Kewzing family
experiences.best_time: September to November for cardamom; March–April for planting
experiences.cost: Included in most homestay stays; tip welcome
experiences.summary: Spend a morning in the fields with your host family: picking large cardamom in the shaded gullies in autumn, sorting and drying pods, or planting and weeding in spring. A practical look at the crop that pays for much of rural Sikkim.
body: Large cardamom, sold as black cardamom, is the main cash crop in many South Sikkim villages, and Sikkim is India's largest producer. It grows as tall clumps in the shade of alder and other trees in damp gullies. The pods form at the base of the plant and are cut by hand, usually from about August to November.

If you are here in harvest season, your hosts may take you down to their plot to pick, then show you the bhatti, a kiln where the pods are dried over wood smoke for a couple of days. That smoke gives Sikkim's cardamom its flavour. Outside harvest, you might help with planting, weeding, milking or making butter tea.

This is joining in, not a staged activity, so follow your hosts' lead and accept if a task is not suitable. Wear clothes you do not mind getting dirty, sturdy shoes and long sleeves in the gullies. A small thank-you to the family, or buying cardamom from them, is appreciated.

faqs.q: When is the cardamom harvest in Sikkim?
faqs.a: Usually from about August to November, varying with altitude and season. Lower plots are picked first. Drying in wood-fired kilns follows the picking, so October and November are good months to see the whole process. Ask your homestay host what stage the harvest will be at during your stay.

faqs.q: Can we buy cardamom from Kewzing farmers?
faqs.a: Often yes, directly from your host family or neighbours, in small quantities for home use. Prices follow the market and change from year to year, so ask the going rate. Dried pods keep for months in an airtight container and make a good, light gift to take home.

faqs.q: Is the farm day suitable for children?
faqs.a: Yes, children usually enjoy it, especially sorting pods, feeding animals or helping in the kitchen garden. The cardamom gullies can be steep, damp and leechy, so keep younger children on the flatter fields. Bring long trousers, closed shoes and insect repellent.

experiences.title: Butter tea, churpi and a Bhutia home kitchen
experiences.summary: Join your hosts in the kitchen to watch or help make suja, the salted butter tea of Bhutia homes, and a simple evening meal. Taste churpi, home pickles and seasonal greens, and learn what a Sikkimese farm kitchen cooks from its own fields.
body: In many Bhutia homes the day runs on suja, tea churned with butter and salt. Traditionally it was made in a tall wooden churn; today many families use a flask or a blender. It tastes more like a light broth than sweet tea, and it is offered to guests as a sign of welcome.

Your hosts may also show you churpi, cheese made from cow milk that is eaten soft in curries or dried hard for chewing, along with home pickles of radish, bamboo shoot or dalle chilli. Dinner is usually rice, dal, a vegetable or meat curry and a seasonal green such as squash shoots, nettle or fiddlehead fern.

Cooking times follow the household, so ask in the morning if you would like to join in the evening. Tell your hosts in advance about vegetarian or other dietary needs. Wash your hands first, keep out from behind the stove unless invited, and say thank you with a clear plate.

faqs.q: What does butter tea taste like?
faqs.a: Salty, rich and warming, closer to a light soup than to sweet milk tea. Many first-timers are surprised, then enjoy it on a cold evening. In Sikkim it is called suja. Your hosts will not mind if you prefer sweet tea instead, but try a cup first.

faqs.q: Is homestay food in Kewzing vegetarian-friendly?
faqs.a: Yes. Rice, dal, vegetables, greens, potatoes and pickles are everyday fare, and meat is easy to leave out. Tell your hosts before you arrive if you are vegetarian, vegan or avoid egg, onion or garlic, so they can plan the household meal accordingly.

faqs.q: What is churpi?
faqs.a: Churpi is a cheese made in Sikkim from cow milk, or yak milk at higher altitudes. Soft churpi is used fresh in curries and soups. Hard churpi is dried into small cubes and chewed slowly for a long time. It keeps for months and travels well.

faqs.q: Is Kewzing worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes, for travellers who want a real village stay rather than a hotel. Kewzing has a well-organised community homestay programme, a Bon monastery that is rare in India, easy village walks and a short drive to Ravangla's sights. It is quiet: come for conversation, farms and views rather than a sightseeing list.

faqs.q: How far is Kewzing from Ravangla?
faqs.a: About 9–10 km, around 20–25 minutes by car, on the road from Ravangla towards Legship. A reserved small car costs about ₹600–900, and shared jeeps on the Ravangla–Legship road pass through for around ₹50–100 a seat. Fares are indicative; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How do Kewzing homestays work?
faqs.a: Since 2003 the village has run a community programme in which an elected committee shares guests between participating families. You stay in a family home, usually with an attached bathroom, and eat meals with or prepared by your hosts. Expect about ₹1,500–2,500 per person a night with meals.

faqs.q: How far is Kewzing from Gangtok?
faqs.a: About 75 km, roughly 3–3.5 hours by road via Singtam and Ravangla. A reserved small car costs about ₹4,000–5,000 one way. On a budget, take a shared jeep from Gangtok to Ravangla, about ₹250–400, then a local jeep or taxi down to Kewzing.

faqs.q: Can we visit Kewzing on the way from Pelling to Namchi?
faqs.a: Yes, it fits naturally. The road from Pelling runs via Legship and climbs through Kewzing to Ravangla, then on to Namchi. A night in Kewzing breaks the drive into two easy halves and lets you see Buddha Park and Ralang without staying in a busier town.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Kewzing?
faqs.a: October to December for clear views and the end of the cardamom harvest, and March to May for warm days and spring flowers. Winter nights are cold but days are sunny. June to September is the monsoon, with heavy rain, leeches on field paths and occasional road slips.

faqs.q: Do we need a permit for Kewzing?
faqs.a: Indians need no permit. Foreign nationals need the standard Sikkim Restricted Area Permit, applied online through the e-FRRO portal since January 2026, but no extra protected-area permit for Kewzing. Homestays collect Sikkim's ₹50 per tourist entry fee. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Kewzing good for families with children?
faqs.a: Yes. The village is safe and quiet, altitude is low at about 1,550 m, and children usually enjoy farm animals, fields and helping in the kitchen. Rooms are simple, so pack a torch, warm layers and any snacks your children rely on. Medical care is in Ravangla or Namchi.

faqs.q: What is there to do in Kewzing?
faqs.a: Walk the village trail linking monasteries and viewpoints, visit the Bon monastery, join your hosts in the fields or kitchen, and in autumn watch cardamom being dried. Day trips to Buddha Park, Ralang, Borong and Temi tea garden are easy by car. Most guests simply slow down for a day.
